label: main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{main}
Assume that $N\geqslant1$ and
\begin{equation}\label{q}
1+\frac1N<q
\quad\text{if }N\in\{1,2\},
\qquad
1+\frac1N<q<\frac{N}{N-2}
\quad\text{if }N\geqslant3.
\end{equation}
Let
\begin{equation}\label{u0}
u_0(x)
=
\frac{C(x)}{|x|^{\frac1{q-1}}},
\qquad
C\in L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^N),
\qquad
C(\lambda x)=C(x)
\end{equation}
for every $\lambda>0$ and a.e. $x\in\mathbb{R}^N$.
Then the Cauchy problem
\begin{equation}\label{eq:main}
\begin{aligned}
u_t-\Delta u+\partial_{x_1}\bigl(|u|^{q-1}u\bigr)&=0,
&&x\in\mathbb{R}^N,\quad t>0,\\
u(x,0)&=u_0(x),
&&x\in\mathbb{R}^N,
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
has a self-similar solution
\begin{equation}\label{u:self:main}
u(x,t)
=
t^{-\frac1{2(q-1)}}
U\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt t}\right),
\end{equation}
where the profile $U=U(x)$ satisfies, in a weak sense,  the elliptic equation
\begin{equation}\label{ell_U_q}
-\Delta U-\frac12x\cdot\nabla U
-\frac{1}{2(q-1)}U
+\partial_{x_1}\bigl(|U|^{q-1}U\bigr)=0
\qquad\text{in }\mathbb{R}^N.
\end{equation}
Moreover, writing
\(
U_0=e^\Delta u_0,
\) 
the following properties hold:
\begin{itemize}
\item
if
\(
q>1+\frac2N,
\)
then
\(
U-U_0\in W^{1,2}(\mathbb{R}^N);
\)

\item
if
\(
1+\frac1N<q\leqslant1+\frac2N,
\)
then
\(
U-U_0\in W^{1,p}(\mathbb{R}^N)
\)
for every
\[
\max\left\{
1,\frac{N(q-1)}q
\right\}
<p<N(q-1).
\]
\end{itemize}
In addition,
\(U\in L^p(\mathbb{R}^N)\) for every
\(p\in\bigl(N(q-1),\infty\bigr]\),
and the initial condition is attained in the sense that
\begin{equation}\label{initial:trace:main}
u(\cdot,t)\longrightarrow u_0
\qquad\text{in }L^r_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}^N)
\quad\text{as }t\to0
\end{equation}
for every
\(
1\leqslant r<N(q-1).
\)
head: environment

label: rem:Lp:self
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:Lp:self}
Here, we record the natural integrability threshold for the self-similar profiles $U = U(x)$. The profiles constructed in Theorem~\ref{main} exhibit a structural barrier to fast spatial decay. Indeed, let $U$ be a bounded, sufficiently smooth solution to the profile equation~\eqref{ell_U_q} such that $U \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^N)$ for some $p > 1$. Testing equation \eqref{ell_U_q} against $|U|^{p-2}U$ and integrating over $\mathbb{R}^N$  (in the same way as in Lemma~\ref{lem:large:p:U}, below) yields
\begin{equation}\label{est:Lp:0}
\frac{4(p-1)}{p^2} \left\| \nabla |U|^{\frac{p}{2}} \right\|_2^2 + \left( \frac{N}{2p} - \frac{1}{2(q-1)} \right) \|U\|_p^p = 0,
\end{equation}
where the convection term vanishes identically upon integration by parts. Consequently, if
$                   
p \le N(q-1),
$                 
both terms in \eqref{est:Lp:0} are non-negative, forcing $U \equiv 0$. Thus, any nontrivial profile $U$ satisfying \eqref{est:Lp:0} must obey
\begin{equation*}
U \notin L^p(\mathbb{R}^N) \qquad \text{for all } 1 < p \le N(q-1).
\end{equation*}
In particular, when $q \ge 1 + \frac{2}{N}$, it follows that $U \notin L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)$. 

This cutoff matches the linear heat-profile estimate in Lemma~\ref{heat_L}, which yields $e^{\Delta} u_0 \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^N)$ for every $p>N(q-1)$.
This threshold aligns with the expected far-field asymptotics of $U(x)$. Because the initial datum $u_0$ is homogeneous of degree $-1/(q-1)$, one naturally expects $U$ to share the leading-order decay rate at spatial infinity:
$
U(x) = \mathcal{O}\!\left(|x|^{-{1}/(q-1)}\right)
$
as $ |x| \to \infty$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Let us explain the restriction
\(
q<{N}/({N-2})
\)
for 
$N\geqslant3$ in Theorem \ref{main}.
In the energy argument, \(V=U-U_0\) belongs to
\(W^{1,2}(\mathbb{R}^N)\). To use
\(\varphi\in W^{1,2}(\mathbb{R}^N)\) as a test function, we need
\(
\psi(U)\in L^2(\mathbb{R}^N).
\)
Since \(|\psi(s)|\leqslant |s|^q\), it is sufficient to have
\(U=V+U_0\in L^{2q}(\mathbb{R}^N)\).
The Sobolev embedding
\(
W^{1,2}(\mathbb{R}^N)
\hookrightarrow L^{\frac{2N}{N-2}}(\mathbb{R}^N)
\)
gives \(V\in L^{2q}(\mathbb{R}^N)\) when
\(q\leqslant N/(N-2)\). On the other hand, Lemma \ref{heat_L}
implies that \(U_0\in L^{2q}(\mathbb{R}^N)\) provided
\(
2q>N(q-1),
\)
or equivalently,
\(
q<{N}/({N-2}).
\)
                                                      
                                                               
Thus, the strict upper bound on \(q\) ensures that the nonlinear
term
\(
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}
\psi(U)\,\partial_{x_1}\varphi\,\,\mathrm d x
\)
is well defined for  \(\varphi \in W^{1,2}(\mathbb{R}^N)\).

label: existence_I
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{existence_I}
Assume $N\geqslant1$ and
\[
1+\frac1N<q
\quad\text{if }N\in\{1,2\},
\qquad
1+\frac1N<q<\frac{N}{N-2}
\quad\text{if }N\geqslant3.
\]
Let $u_0$ be of the form \eqref{u0}, and let $\psi$ be given by
formula \eqref{psi1} with an arbitrary $A>0$. Then equation
\eqref{ell_V:gen} has a weak solution $V=V(x)$ with the following
properties:
\begin{itemize}
\item
if
\(
q>1+\frac2N,
\)
then
\(
V\in W^{1,2}(\mathbb{R}^N);
\)
\item
if
\(
q\in\left(1+\frac1N,1+\frac2N\right],
\)
then
\[
V\in W^{1,p}(\mathbb{R}^N)
\qquad\text{for every}\qquad
\max\left\{1,\frac{N(q-1)}{q}\right\}
<p<N(q-1).
\]
\end{itemize}

label: C_omega:1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{C_omega:1} Let $N\geq 1$.
Let $q\geqslant 1+\frac{2}{N}$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^N$ be a bounded
domain with $C^2$ boundary,
let $u_0$ be defined by \eqref{u0} and 
let $U_0=e^\Delta u_0$, and let
\(\psi\in W^{1,\infty}(\mathbb{R})\) be arbitrary.
Then the boundary value problem
\begin{align}\label{ell:bounded_4}
-\Delta V-\frac{x}{2}\cdot\nabla V-\frac{1}{2(q-1)}V
+\partial_{x_1}\psi(V+U_0)&=0,
&&x\in\Omega,\\
V&=0,
&&x\in\partial\Omega,
\end{align}
has a weak solution $V\in W^{1,2}_0(\Omega)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Set
\[
c=\frac{1}{2(q-1)}.
\]
For \(W\in W^{1,2}_0(\Omega)\), define \(T(W)=Z\), where \(Z\in
W^{1,2}_0(\Omega)\) is the unique weak solution of
\[
-\Delta Z
=
\frac{x}{2}\cdot\nabla W+cW
-\partial_{x_1}\psi(W+U_0),
\qquad
Z|_{\partial\Omega}=0.
\]
Since \(\psi\in L^\infty(\mathbb{R})\), the right-hand side belongs to
\(W^{-1,2}(\Omega)\), and hence \(T\) is well defined by the
Lax--Milgram theorem.

The map
\(
T:W^{1,2}_0(\Omega)\longrightarrow W^{1,2}_0(\Omega)
\)
is continuous and compact. Indeed, continuity follows from the Lipschitz
continuity of \(\psi\) and the continuity of the inverse Dirichlet
Laplacian. To prove compactness, write \(T=T_1+T_2\), where
\[
T_1(W)
=
(-\Delta_D)^{-1}
\left(\frac{x}{2}\cdot\nabla W+cW\right),
\qquad
T_2(W)
=
(-\Delta_D)^{-1}
\left(-\partial_{x_1}\psi(W+U_0)\right).
\]
The map \(T_1\) is compact from \(W^{1,2}_0(\Omega)\) into itself by
elliptic \(W^{2,2}\)-regularity and the compact embedding
\(W^{2,2}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow W^{1,2}(\Omega)\). Moreover, if
\(\{W_n\}\) is bounded in \(W^{1,2}_0(\Omega)\), then, after passing to a
subsequence,
\(
W_n\to W
\)
in $L^2(\Omega)$.
Since \(\psi\) is globally Lipschitz,
\[
\psi(W_n+U_0)\to\psi(W+U_0)
\qquad\text{in }L^2(\Omega),
\]
and therefore \(T_2(W_n)\to T_2(W)\) in \(W^{1,2}_0(\Omega)\). Thus \(T\)
is compact.

It remains to obtain the Leray--Schauder {\it a priori} bound. Let
\(
V=\lambda T(V)
\)
for $\lambda \in [0,1]$.
Then
\[
-\Delta V
=
\lambda\left(
\frac{x}{2}\cdot\nabla V+cV
-\partial_{x_1}\psi(V+U_0)
\right).
\]
This equation holds in $\Omega$, together with the homogeneous Dirichlet
boundary condition.
Testing this equation with \(V\) and using the relation
\[
\frac12\int_\Omega (x\cdot\nabla V)V\,\,\mathrm d x
=
-\frac N4\int_\Omega V^2\,\,\mathrm d x,
\]
we obtain
\[
\|\nabla V\|_2^2
+
\lambda\left(
\frac N4-\frac{1}{2(q-1)}
\right)\|V\|_2^2
=
\lambda\int_\Omega
\psi(V+U_0)\partial_{x_1}V\,\,\mathrm d x.
\]
Since \(q\geq 1+2/N\), the second term on the left-hand side is
nonnegative. Hence
\[
\|\nabla V\|_2^2
\leqslant
|\Omega|^{1/2}\|\psi\|_\infty\|\nabla V\|_2,
\]
and consequently
\(
\|\nabla V\|_2
\leqslant
|\Omega|^{1/2}\|\psi\|_\infty.
\)
By the Poincar\'e inequality, this gives a bound for \(V\) in
\(W^{1,2}_0(\Omega)\), uniform with respect to \(\lambda\in[0,1]\).
The Leray--Schauder theorem therefore yields a fixed point
\(V\in W^{1,2}_0(\Omega)\) of \(T\), which is a weak solution of
\eqref{ell:bounded_4}.
head: environment

label: lemma_1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma_1}
Let $1<p<2$ and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^N$ be an arbitrary domain.
Suppose that
\[
|V|^{\frac p2-1}V\in W^{1,2}_0(\Omega).
\]
Then $V\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ and
\begin{equation}\label{lemma_1:estimate}
\int_\Omega |\nabla V|^p\,\mathrm d x
\leqslant
C(p)
\left(
\int_\Omega
\left|\nabla\big(|V|^{\frac p2-1}V\big)\right|^2\,\mathrm d x
+
\int_\Omega |V|^p\,\mathrm d x
\right).
\end{equation}
If, in addition, $\Omega$ is bounded, then
\begin{equation}\label{lemma_1:estimate:bounded}
\int_\Omega |\nabla V|^p\,\mathrm d x
\leqslant
C(p,\Omega)
\int_\Omega
\left|\nabla\big(|V|^{\frac p2-1}V\big)\right|^2\,\mathrm d x.
\end{equation}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Set
\[
w=|V|^{\frac p2-1}V,
\quad 
\text{then}
\quad 
V=|w|^{\frac2p-1}w.
\]
For smooth $w$ we have
\[
|\nabla V|
=
\frac2p |w|^{\frac2p-1}|\nabla w|,
\]
and consequently, by H\"older's inequality,
\begin{align*}
\int_\Omega|\nabla V|^p\,\mathrm d x
&=
\left(\frac2p\right)^p
\int_\Omega
|w|^{2-p}|\nabla w|^p\,\mathrm d x
\\
&\leqslant
\left(\frac2p\right)^p
\left(\int_\Omega|\nabla w|^2\,\mathrm d x\right)^{p/2}
\left(\int_\Omega|w|^2\,\mathrm d x\right)^{(2-p)/2}
\\
&\leqslant
C(p)
\left(
\int_\Omega|\nabla w|^2\,\mathrm d x
+
\int_\Omega|w|^2\,\mathrm d x
\right).
\end{align*}
The general case follows by approximation in $W^{1,2}_0(\Omega)$, which we describe in detail in Lemma \ref{C_psi_1} below.
Since $|w|^2=|V|^p$, this proves inequality \eqref{lemma_1:estimate}.
If $\Omega$ is bounded, inequality \eqref{lemma_1:estimate:bounded} follows
from the Poincar\'e inequality applied to $w$.
head: environment

label: lemma_2
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma_2}
Let
\(
q\in\left(1+\frac1N,1+\frac2N\right]
\)
and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^N$ be a bounded domain with $C^2$ boundary.
Let $\psi\in W^{1,\infty}(\mathbb{R})$ be given by formula \eqref{psi1}  
with some $A>0$. 
Let $u_0$ be defined by \eqref{u0} and set $U_0=e^\Delta u_0$.
For every
\(
1<p<N(q-1),
\)
the boundary value problem
\begin{equation}\label{ell:bounded}
\begin{aligned}
-\Delta V-\frac{x}{2}\cdot\nabla V
-\frac{1}{2(q-1)}V
&=
-\partial_{x_1}\psi (V+e^\Delta u_0),
&&x\in\Omega,\\
V&=0,
&&x\in\partial\Omega,
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
has a weak solution $V\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Set
\[
c=\frac{1}{2(q-1)}\quad \text{and} \qquad X=W^{1,p}_0(\Omega).
\]
Since \(q\leq 1+2/N\) and \(p<N(q-1)\), we have \(1<p<2\).
Moreover, by Lemma \ref{heat_L}, we have 
\(
U_0,\nabla U_0\in L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^N).
\)

For \(W\in X\), let \(T(W)=Z\), where \(Z\in X\) solves
\[
-\Delta Z
=
\frac{x}{2}\cdot\nabla W+cW
-\partial_{x_1}\psi(W+U_0),
\qquad
Z|_{\partial\Omega}=0.
\]
Since \(\psi\) is bounded and globally Lipschitz, standard elliptic
regularity estimates show that \(T:X\to X\) is well defined and continuous.
Moreover, the proof of Lemma~\ref{C_omega:1} shows that \(T\) is compact.
                                   
                                                                    
                                                                           
                                                                       
                                                           
                                 

We apply the Leray--Schauder theorem. Let
\(
V=\lambda T(V)
\)
for $\lambda \in [0,1]$.
Then
\begin{equation}\label{ell:bounded:homotopy:p}
-\Delta V
=
\lambda\left(
\frac{x}{2}\cdot\nabla V+cV
-\partial_{x_1}\psi(V+U_0)
\right).
\end{equation}
Standard elliptic bootstrap, using the chain rule in the nonlinear term and the boundedness of \(\psi'\), yields
enough regularity to justify the calculations below.
               
                                                                  
                 
Using a standard regularization of \(|V|^{p-2}V\) as a test function in
equation
\eqref{ell:bounded:homotopy:p} 
and then passing to the limit
(see the proof of Lemma \ref{C_psi_1} below for more detailed reasoning), we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{p_est_correct}
\begin{split}
&\frac{4(p-1)}{p^2}
\int_\Omega
\left|
\nabla\bigl(|V|^{\frac p2-1}V\bigr)
\right|^2\,\mathrm d x
+
\lambda\left(
\frac{N}{2p}-\frac{1}{2(q-1)}
\right)
\int_\Omega |V|^p\,\mathrm d x
\\
&\qquad\leqslant
\lambda
\left|
\int_\Omega
\psi'(V+U_0)
\bigl(\partial_{x_1}V+\partial_{x_1}U_0\bigr)
|V|^{p-2}V\,\,\mathrm d x
\right|.
\end{split}
\end{equation}
Here we used
\[
\frac12\int_\Omega
(x\cdot\nabla V)|V|^{p-2}V\,\,\mathrm d x
=
-\frac{N}{2p}\int_\Omega |V|^p\,\,\mathrm d x.
\]
Since \(p<N(q-1)\), the second term on the left-hand side of
\eqref{p_est_correct} is nonnegative.

By the definition \eqref{psi1} of the truncated nonlinearity,
\[
\psi'(V+U_0)=0
\qquad\text{a.e. on }\{|V+U_0|>A\}.
\]
Consequently, on the support of \(\psi'(V+U_0)\), we have
\(
|V|\leq A+\|U_0\|_\infty,
\)
and therefore
\[
\left|
\int_\Omega
\psi'(V+U_0)
\bigl(\partial_{x_1}V+\partial_{x_1}U_0\bigr)
|V|^{p-2}V\,\,\mathrm d x
\right|
\leq
C\left(
\|\nabla V\|_{L^1(\Omega)}+1
\right),
\]
where   \(C=C(U_0,|\Omega|,A)>0\) is independent of \(\lambda\).

Set
\[
E=
\int_\Omega
\left|
\nabla\bigl(|V|^{\frac p2-1}V\bigr)
\right|^2\,\mathrm d x.
\]
By Lemma \ref{lemma_1},
\[
\|\nabla V\|_p^p\leq C E,
\]
and hence
\[
\|\nabla V\|_1
\leq
C\|\nabla V\|_p
\leq C E^{1/p}.
\]
Dropping the nonnegative \(L^p\)-term in \eqref{p_est_correct}, we obtain
\[
E\leq C E^{1/p}+C.
\]
Since \(p>1\), the $\varepsilon$-Young inequality gives
\(
E\leq C,
\)
uniformly with respect to \(\lambda\in[0,1]\). Lemma \ref{lemma_1} and
the Poincar\'e inequality then yield
\(
\|V\|_{W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)}
\leq C,
\)
again independently of \(\lambda\).
Thus all the assumptions of the Leray--Schauder theorem are satisfied.
Hence \(T\) has a fixed point \(V\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)\), which is a weak
solution of \eqref{ell:bounded}.

label: C_psi
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{C_psi}
Assume that
\[
q>1+\frac{2}{N}
\quad\text{if }N\in\{1,2\},
\qquad
1+\frac{2}{N}<q<\frac{N}{N-2}
\quad\text{if }N\geqslant3.
\]
Let $\psi=\psi_A$ be the truncated nonlinearity defined in
\eqref{psi1}, with an arbitrary truncation level $A>0$. Let
$u_0$ be given by \eqref{u0} and set
\(
U_0=e^\Delta u_0.
\)
Then, for every $k\in\mathbb N$, the boundary value problem
\eqref{Vk_equ} has a weak solution
\(
V_k\in W^{1,2}_0(B_k).
\)
Moreover, there exists a constant
\(
C=C(A,N,q,U_0)>0,
\)
independent of $k$ and of the chosen solution $V_k$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{Vk_psi}
\|\nabla V_k\|_{L^2(B_k)}^2
+
\|V_k\|_{L^2(B_k)}^2
\leqslant C.
\end{equation}

If, in addition,
$                                            
1+\frac{2}{N}<q<2,
$                
then the constant in inequality  \eqref{Vk_psi} can be chosen in the form
\(
C=C(N,q,U_0),
\)
and is therefore independent of both $k$ and the truncation level
$A$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The existence of $V_k$ follows from Lemma \ref{C_omega:1}.
It remains to prove the stated estimates.
Set
\[
\alpha
=
\frac{N}{4}-\frac{1}{2(q-1)}.
\]
The assumption $q>1+2/N$ implies that
$                                     
\alpha>0.
$                

Testing equation \eqref{Vk_equ} with $V_k$ and using
$V_k=0$ on $\partial B_k$, we obtain
\begin{align}
\|\nabla V_k\|_{L^2(B_k)}^2
+
\alpha\|V_k\|_{L^2(B_k)}^2
&=
\int_{B_k}
\psi_A(V_k+U_0)\,
\partial_{x_1}V_k\,dx.
\label{C_psi:energy}
\end{align}
         
    
                    
                           
   
                                   
    

Let
\(
\Psi_A(s)=\int_0^s\psi_A(z)\,dz.
\)
Since $\psi_A$ is globally Lipschitz, the Sobolev chain rule gives
\[
\partial_{x_1}\Psi_A(V_k)
=
\psi_A(V_k)\partial_{x_1}V_k
\qquad\text{a.e. in }B_k.
\]
Because $V_k=0$ on $\partial B_k$ and $\Psi_A(0)=0$, integration
by parts yields
\[
\int_{B_k}
\psi_A(V_k)\partial_{x_1}V_k\,dx
=
\int_{B_k}\partial_{x_1}\Psi_A(V_k)\,dx
=
0.
\]
Consequently,
\begin{align}
\left|
\int_{B_k}
\psi_A(V_k+U_0)\partial_{x_1}V_k\,dx
\right|
&=
\left|
\int_{B_k}
\bigl(
\psi_A(V_k+U_0)-\psi_A(V_k)
\bigr)
\partial_{x_1}V_k\,dx
\right|.
\label{C_psi:difference}
\end{align}

The truncations $\psi_A$ satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{C_psi:uniform-difference}
|\psi_A(a+b)-\psi_A(a)|
\leqslant
C(q)|b|
\bigl(
|a|^{q-1}+|b|^{q-1}
\bigr),
\end{equation}
where $C(q)$ is independent of $A$. Applying
\eqref{C_psi:uniform-difference} with $a=V_k$ and $b=U_0$ gives
\begin{align}
&\left|
\int_{B_k}
\bigl(
\psi_A(V_k+U_0)-\psi_A(V_k)
\bigr)
\partial_{x_1}V_k\,dx
\right|
\nonumber\\
&\qquad\qquad
\leqslant
C(q)\int_{B_k}
\left(
|U_0|^q
+
|U_0||V_k|^{q-1}
\right)
|\nabla V_k|\,dx.
\label{C_psi:basic-estimate}
\end{align}

We first consider the subquadratic case
$1+\frac{2}{N}<q<2$.
For every $\varepsilon>0$, the $\varepsilon$-Young inequality gives
\begin{align}
\int_{B_k}|U_0|^q|\nabla V_k|\,dx
&\leqslant
\varepsilon\|\nabla V_k\|_{L^2(B_k)}^2
+
C(\varepsilon)
\|U_0\|_{L^{2q}(\mathbb R^N)}^{2q}.
\label{C_psi:U0q}
\end{align}

For the second term, use the $\varepsilon$-Young inequality with the three
conjugate exponents
$
{2}/({2-q}),
$ 
$
{2}/({q-1}),
$ and 
$
2.
$
                            
    
               
   
               
   
         
     
    
After inserting suitable $\varepsilon$-factors, we obtain
\begin{align}
|U_0||V_k|^{q-1}|\nabla V_k|
&\leqslant
C(\varepsilon,q)
|U_0|^{\frac{2}{2-q}}
+
\varepsilon |V_k|^2
+
\varepsilon|\nabla V_k|^2.
\end{align}
Therefore,
\begin{align}
\int_{B_k}
|U_0||V_k|^{q-1}|\nabla V_k|\,dx
&\leqslant
\varepsilon
\left(
\|V_k\|_{L^2(B_k)}^2
+
\|\nabla V_k\|_{L^2(B_k)}^2
\right)
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
C(\varepsilon,q)
\|U_0\|_{
L^{\frac{2}{2-q}}(\mathbb R^N)
}^{\frac{2}{2-q}}.
\label{C_psi:mixed-subquadratic}
\end{align}


The two norms of $U_0$ appearing above are finite. Indeed, the
heat-profile estimate in Lemma \ref{heat_L} gives
\(
U_0\in L^r(\mathbb R^N)
\)
whenever
\(
r>N(q-1).
\)
First, the inequality
\(
2q>N(q-1)
\)
is equivalent, for $N\geqslant3$, to
\(
q<\frac{N}{N-2}.
\)
Second, to verify the inequality 
\(
\frac{2}{2-q}>N(q-1),
\)
observe that
\(
q-1<\frac{2}{N-2}
\)
by the upper restriction on $q$, while
\(
2-q<\frac{N-2}{N}
\)
because $q>1+2/N$. Hence
\[
(q-1)(2-q)
<
\frac{2}{N-2}\frac{N-2}{N}
=
\frac2N,
\]
which is equivalent to
\(
\frac{2}{2-q}>N(q-1).
\)

Combining \eqref{C_psi:energy},
\eqref{C_psi:difference}, \eqref{C_psi:basic-estimate},
\eqref{C_psi:U0q}, and
\eqref{C_psi:mixed-subquadratic}, we obtain
\begin{align}
\|\nabla V_k\|_2^2+\alpha\|V_k\|_2^2
&\leqslant
C(q)\varepsilon
\left(
\|\nabla V_k\|_2^2+\|V_k\|_2^2
\right)
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
C(\varepsilon,q)
\left(
\|U_0\|_{2q}^{2q}
+
\|U_0\|_{\frac{2}{2-q}}^{\frac{2}{2-q}}
\right).
\label{C_psi:subquadratic-final}
\end{align}
Choosing $\varepsilon>0$ sufficiently small
      
    
                 
   
                          
    
and absorbing the first term on the right-hand side into the
left-hand side, we obtain
\[
\|\nabla V_k\|_{L^2(B_k)}^2
+
\|V_k\|_{L^2(B_k)}^2
\leqslant
C(N,q,U_0).
\]
Every constant used in this part is independent of $A$.
This proves the asserted truncation-independent estimate when
$1+2/N<q<2$.

It remains to discuss the case $q\geqslant2$. For this range the
argument gives an estimate for each fixed $A$, but not an estimate
uniform in $A$.
Set
\[
M=A+\|U_0\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb R^N)}
\]
and
\[
\Omega_{k,A}
=
\{x\in B_k:\ |V_k(x)|\leqslant M\}.
\]
If $x\in B_k\setminus\Omega_{k,A}$, then $V_k(x)$ and
$V_k(x)+U_0(x)$ have the same sign and both have absolute value
larger than $A$. Hence
\[
\psi_A(V_k+U_0)=\psi_A(V_k)
\qquad\text{on }B_k\setminus\Omega_{k,A}.
\]
Thus the integral in \eqref{C_psi:difference} is supported in
$\Omega_{k,A}$.

Fix $R>0$. On $\Omega_{k,A}\cap B_R$, the estimate
$\|\psi_A\|_\infty\leqslant A^q$ gives
\begin{align}
&\left|
\int_{\Omega_{k,A}\cap B_R}
\bigl(
\psi_A(V_k+U_0)-\psi_A(V_k)
\bigr)
\partial_{x_1}V_k\,dx
\right|
\nonumber\\
&\qquad
\leqslant
2A^q|B_R|^{1/2}
\|\nabla V_k\|_{L^2(B_k)}
\nonumber\\
&\qquad
\leqslant
\varepsilon\|\nabla V_k\|_{L^2(B_k)}^2
+
C(\varepsilon)A^{2q}|B_R|.
\label{C_psi:local-A}
\end{align}
This term already exhibits explicit dependence on $A$.

On $\Omega_{k,A}$ we have $|V_k|\leqslant M$, and hence, because
$q\geqslant2$, we obtain
\[
|V_k|^{q-1}
\leqslant
M^{q-2}|V_k|.
\]
It follows that
\begin{align}
&\int_{\Omega_{k,A}\cap B_R^c}
|U_0||V_k|^{q-1}|\nabla V_k|\,dx
\nonumber\\
&\qquad
\leqslant
\frac{M^{q-2}}{2}
\|U_0\|_{L^\infty(B_R^c)}
\left(
\|V_k\|_{L^2(B_k)}^2
+
\|\nabla V_k\|_{L^2(B_k)}^2
\right).
\label{C_psi:exterior-A}
\end{align}
Since
\(
\|U_0\|_{L^\infty(B_R^c)}
\to 0
\)
as $R\to \infty$,
we may choose $R$ sufficiently large that the coefficient in
\eqref{C_psi:exterior-A} can be absorbed into the left-hand side
of \eqref{C_psi:energy}. In general, this choice depends on
\[
M^{q-2}
=
\bigl(
A+\|U_0\|_\infty
\bigr)^{q-2},
\]
and therefore depends on $A$ when $q>2$.

The remaining exterior term is estimated by
\[
\int_{B_k}|U_0|^q|\nabla V_k|\,dx
\leqslant
\varepsilon\|\nabla V_k\|_2^2
+
C(\varepsilon)\|U_0\|_{2q}^{2q}.
\]
Choosing first $R$ and then $\varepsilon$ sufficiently small and
absorbing the energy terms, we obtain
\[
\|\nabla V_k\|_{L^2(B_k)}^2
+
\|V_k\|_{L^2(B_k)}^2
\leqslant
C(A,N,q,U_0).
\]
The constant is independent of $k$ and $V_k$, but the argument
does not make it independent of $A$. The dependence on $A$ occurs
explicitly in \eqref{C_psi:local-A} and, for $q>2$, also in the
choice of $R$ following inequality \eqref{C_psi:exterior-A}.

label: C_psi_1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{C_psi_1}
Let $N\geqslant1$ and assume that
\(
q\in\left(1+\frac1N,\,1+\frac2N\right].
\)
Let
\[
\max\left\{
1,\frac{N(q-1)}q
\right\}
<p<N(q-1),
\]
and let $\psi=\psi_A$ be the truncated nonlinearity defined by \eqref{psi1} with a truncation level $A>0$.
Let $u_0$ be defined by \eqref{u0}, set
\(
U_0=e^\Delta u_0,
\)
and suppose that
\(
V_k\in W^{1,p}_0(B_k)
\)
is a weak solution of
\begin{equation}\label{ell:bounded:uni:p:Cpsi1}
\begin{aligned}
-\Delta V_k-\frac{x}{2}\cdot\nabla V_k
-\frac{1}{2(q-1)}V_k
+\partial_{x_1}\psi_A(V_k+U_0)&=0
&&\text{in }B_k,\\
V_k&=0
&&\text{on }\partial B_k.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}\label{Cpsi1:estimate}
\|V_k\|_{W^{1,p}_0(B_k)}
\leqslant
C(A,N,q,p,U_0),
\end{equation}
where the constant is independent of $k$ and of the particular
solution $V_k$.

Moreover, if
\(
N\geqslant2
\)
and
\(
q<2,
\)
then the constant in \eqref{Cpsi1:estimate} can be chosen
independently of the truncation level $A$.

title: Proof
body_md:
For simplicity, write
\[
V=V_k
\qquad\text{and}\qquad 
c=\frac{1}{2(q-1)}.
\]
All constants below are independent of $k$.

In the following reasoning, we present a regularization procedure which allows us to obtain $W^{1,p}$-estimates for $p\in (1,2)$ in this proof as well as in other parts of this paper.
For $\delta>0$, define
\[
\Phi_\delta(s)
=
s(s^2+\delta)^{\frac{p-2}{2}},
\qquad
Q_\delta(s)
=
\int_0^s\Phi_\delta(\tau)\,\,\mathrm d\tau.
\]
Then $\Phi_\delta$ is increasing and
\begin{equation}\label{Cpsi1:Phi-properties}
0\leqslant\Phi_\delta'(s)
\leqslant C(p)|s|^{p-2},
\qquad s\neq0.
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\[
\Phi_\delta(s)\longrightarrow |s|^{p-2}s,
\qquad
Q_\delta(s)\longrightarrow \frac1p|s|^p
\]
as $\delta\downarrow0$.
Testing the boundary value problem \eqref{ell:bounded:uni:p:Cpsi1} with
$\Phi_\delta(V)$ gives
\begin{align}
&\int_{B_k}\Phi_\delta'(V)|\nabla V|^2\,dx
+\frac N2\int_{B_k}Q_\delta(V)\,dx
-c\int_{B_k}V\Phi_\delta(V)\,dx
\nonumber\\
&\qquad
=
\int_{B_k}
\psi_A(V+U_0)\Phi_\delta'(V)\,
\partial_{x_1}V\,dx.
\label{Cpsi1:regularized-energy}
\end{align}
                                                                
                                  
                                  

Introduce
\[
P_\delta(v,u)
=
\int_0^v
\psi_A(s+u)\Phi_\delta'(s)\,ds.
\]
Then
\[
\partial_vP_\delta(v,u)
=
\psi_A(v+u)\Phi_\delta'(v).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\partial_{x_1}P_\delta(V,U_0)
=
\psi_A(V+U_0)\Phi_\delta'(V)\partial_{x_1}V
+
\partial_uP_\delta(V,U_0)\partial_{x_1}U_0.
\]
Because \(V=0\) on \(\partial B_k\) and
\(P_\delta(0,u)=0\), integration over \(B_k\) gives
\begin{equation}\label{Cpsi1:P-integration}
\int_{B_k}
\psi_A(V+U_0)\Phi_\delta'(V)\partial_{x_1}V\,dx
=
-\int_{B_k}
\partial_uP_\delta(V,U_0)\partial_{x_1}U_0\,dx.
\end{equation}
Combining \eqref{Cpsi1:regularized-energy} and
\eqref{Cpsi1:P-integration}, we obtain
\begin{align}
&\int_{B_k}\Phi_\delta'(V)|\nabla V|^2\,dx
+\frac N2\int_{B_k}Q_\delta(V)\,dx
-c\int_{B_k}V\Phi_\delta(V)\,dx
\nonumber\\
&\qquad
=
-\int_{B_k}
\partial_uP_\delta(V,U_0)\partial_{x_1}U_0\,dx.
\label{Cpsi1:regularized-energy:P}
\end{align}

 We next estimate the last integral using
      
    
            
   
                                  
                                      
    
          
the truncation-independent pointwise estimate
$                                                 
|\psi_A'(z)|
\leqslant q|z|^{q-1}.
$                
Therefore, by \eqref{Cpsi1:Phi-properties},
\begin{align}
|\partial_uP_\delta(v,u)|
&=
\left|
\int_0^v
\psi_A'(s+u)\Phi_\delta'(s)\,ds
\right|
\nonumber\\
&\leqslant
C(p,q)
\int_0^{|v|}
(s+|u|)^{q-1}s^{p-2}\,ds
\nonumber\\
&\leqslant
C(p,q)
\left(
|v|^{p+q-2}
+
|u|^{q-1}|v|^{p-1}
\right).
\label{Cpsi1:Pu-uniform}
\end{align}
The constant in \eqref{Cpsi1:Pu-uniform} is independent of
both \(A\) and \(\delta\).

We distinguish the relevant cases.

\medskip
\noindent
\textit{Case 1: \(N\geqslant2\) and \(q<2\).}
Using inequality \eqref{Cpsi1:Pu-uniform}, we obtain
\begin{align}
\left|
\int_{B_k}
\partial_uP_\delta(V,U_0)\partial_{x_1}U_0\,dx
\right|
&\leqslant
C
\int_{B_k}
|\nabla U_0||V|^{p+q-2}\,dx
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
C
\int_{B_k}
|U_0|^{q-1}|\nabla U_0||V|^{p-1}\,dx.
\label{Cpsi1:RHS-two-terms}
\end{align}
The Young inequality gives, for every \(\varepsilon>0\),
\begin{align}
\int_{B_k}
|\nabla U_0||V|^{p+q-2}\,dx
&\leqslant
\varepsilon\|V\|_{L^p(B_k)}^p
+
C_\varepsilon
\|\nabla U_0\|_
 {L^{p/(2-q)}(\mathbb R^N)}^{p/(2-q)},
\label{Cpsi1:first-young}\\
\int_{B_k}
|U_0|^{q-1}|\nabla U_0||V|^{p-1}\,dx
&\leqslant
\varepsilon\|V\|_{L^p(B_k)}^p
+
C_\varepsilon
\bigl\|
 |U_0|^{q-1}\nabla U_0
\bigr\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^N)}^p.
\label{Cpsi1:second-young}
\end{align}
The assumptions on \(p\) imply
\[
\frac{p}{2-q}>N(q-1)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
pq>N(q-1).
\]
Indeed,
\[
p>\frac{N(q-1)}q,
\qquad
q>1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
2-q<\frac1q.
\]
Thus, Lemma \ref{heat_L}
implies 
\[
\nabla U_0\in
L^{p/(2-q)}(\mathbb R^N)
\quad \text{and}\quad 
U_0,\nabla U_0\in L^{pq}(\mathbb R^N).
\]
In particular, the H\"older inequality yields
\[
\bigl\|
 |U_0|^{q-1}\nabla U_0
\bigr\|_{L^p}
\leqslant
\|U_0\|_{L^{pq}}^{q-1}
\|\nabla U_0\|_{L^{pq}}.
\]
It follows from \eqref{Cpsi1:RHS-two-terms}-- 
\eqref{Cpsi1:second-young} that
\begin{equation}\label{Cpsi1:RHS-uniform}
\left|
\int_{B_k}
\partial_uP_\delta(V,U_0)\partial_{x_1}U_0\,dx
\right|
\leqslant
2\varepsilon\|V\|_{L^p(B_k)}^p
+
C_\varepsilon(N,q,p,U_0),
\end{equation}
where the constant is independent of \(A\), \(k\), and
\(\delta\).

Letting \(\delta\downarrow0\) in
\eqref{Cpsi1:regularized-energy:P}, using Fatou's lemma for the
gradient term and the standard convergence of the regularized
powers, gives
\begin{align}
\frac{4(p-1)}{p^2}
\left\|
 \nabla\bigl(|V|^{\frac p2-1}V\bigr)
\right\|_{L^2(B_k)}^2
+
\left(
\frac{N}{2p}-\frac{1}{2(q-1)}
\right)
\|V\|_{L^p(B_k)}^p
\nonumber\\
\leqslant
2\varepsilon\|V\|_{L^p(B_k)}^p
+
C_\varepsilon(N,q,p,U_0).
\label{Cpsi1:limit-energy}
\end{align}
Since \(p<N(q-1)\),
\[
\gamma_p
:=
\frac{N}{2p}-\frac{1}{2(q-1)}
>0.
\]
Choosing \(\varepsilon<\gamma_p/4\) and absorbing the
\(L^p\)-term into the left-hand side, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{Cpsi1:weighted-estimate}
\left\|
 \nabla\bigl(|V|^{\frac p2-1}V\bigr)
\right\|_{L^2(B_k)}^2
+
\|V\|_{L^p(B_k)}^p
\leqslant
C(N,q,p,U_0).
\end{equation}
The constant in \eqref{Cpsi1:weighted-estimate} is independent of
\(A\) and \(k\).

Applying the \(W^{1,p}\)-estimate from Lemma~\ref{lemma_1}, we obtain
\[
\|V\|_{W^{1,p}_0(B_k)}^p
\leqslant
C(p)
\left[
\left\|
 \nabla\bigl(|V|^{\frac p2-1}V\bigr)
\right\|_{L^2(B_k)}^2
+
\|V\|_{L^p(B_k)}^p
\right].
\]
Thus, we conclude that
\[
\|V_k\|_{W^{1,p}_0(B_k)}
\leqslant
C(N,q,p,U_0),
\]
with a constant independent of both \(k\) and \(A\).

\medskip
\noindent
\textit{Case 2: \(N=1\).}
In this case the assumed range of \(q\) is
\(
2<q\leqslant3.
\)
Denote
\(
B=\|U_0\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb R)}.
\)
Because \(\psi_A'(s+u)=0\) whenever \(|s+u|>A\), the integrand
defining \(\partial_uP_\delta(v,u)\) vanishes unless
\(
|s|\leqslant A+B.
\)
Thus
\begin{align}
|\partial_uP_\delta(v,u)|
&\leqslant
C(p)qA^{q-1}
\int_{|s|\leqslant A+B}|s|^{p-2}\,ds
\nonumber\\
&\leqslant
C(p,q)A^{q-1}(A+B)^{p-1}.
\label{Cpsi1:N1-local}
\end{align}
By Lemma \ref{heat_L}, $U_0'\in L^1(\mathbb R)$ and consequently 
\[
\left|
\int_{B_k}
\partial_uP_\delta(V,U_0)U_0'\,dx
\right|
\leqslant
C(A,p,q,U_0)\|U_0'\|_{L^1(\mathbb R)}.
\]
Proceeding as above and using
\[
\frac{1}{2p}-\frac{1}{2(q-1)}>0,
\]
we obtain
\[
\|V_k\|_{W^{1,p}_0(B_k)}
\leqslant
C(A,p,q,U_0).
\]
This bound is independent of \(k\), but the estimate
\eqref{Cpsi1:N1-local} depends on \(A\). 

\medskip
\noindent
\textit{Case 3: \(N=2\) and \(q=2\).}
Here inequality \eqref{Cpsi1:Pu-uniform} becomes
\[
|\partial_uP_\delta(v,u)|
\leqslant
C(p)
\left(
|v|^p+|u||v|^{p-1}
\right).
\]
On the complement of a sufficiently large ball \(B_R\), the
decay of \(\nabla U_0\) allows the term
\[
C\int_{B_k\setminus B_R}
|\nabla U_0||V|^p\,dx
\]
to be absorbed into the left-hand side of the energy estimate.
The remaining term on \(B_k\setminus B_R\) is estimated by
\[
\varepsilon\|V\|_{L^p(B_k)}^p
+
C_\varepsilon
\|U_0\nabla U_0\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^2)}^p.
\]

On the fixed ball \(B_R\), however, one uses the local estimate
\[
|\partial_uP_\delta(v,u)|
\leqslant
C(A,p,\|U_0\|_\infty)|v|^{p-1}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\int_{B_R}
|\partial_uP_\delta(V,U_0)||\nabla U_0|\,dx
\leqslant
\varepsilon\|V\|_{L^p(B_R)}^p
+
C_{\varepsilon,R}(A,p,U_0).
\]
The rest of the argument gives
\[
\|V_k\|_{W^{1,p}_0(B_k)}
\leqslant
C(A,p,U_0),
\]
independently of \(k\).

label: Vk_equ:correct
title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that 
\(
U_0=e^\Delta u_0.
\)
For each $k\in\mathbb{N}$, let $V_k$ be a solution of the Dirichlet
problem
\begin{equation}\label{Vk_equ:correct}
\begin{aligned}
-\Delta V_k-\frac{x}{2}\cdot\nabla V_k
-\frac{1}{2(q-1)}V_k
&=
-\partial_{x_1}\psi(V_k+U_0),
&&x\in B_k,\\
V_k&=0,
&&x\in\partial B_k.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
We extend each $V_k$ by zero outside $B_k$. Since
$V_k\in W^{1,p}_0(B_k)$, its zero extension, still denoted by
$V_k$, belongs to $W^{1,p}(\mathbb{R}^N)$.

We consider separately the two ranges of $q$.

\medskip
\noindent
\textit{Case 1: $q>1+\frac2N$.}
By Lemma \ref{C_psi}, problem \eqref{Vk_equ:correct} has a
solution
\(
V_k\in W^{1,2}_0(B_k).
\)
satisfying 
 the estimate
\(
\|V_k\|_{W^{1,2}(\mathbb{R}^N)}
\leqslant C,
\)
where $C$ is independent of $k$. Thus, after passing to a subsequence, there exists
\(
V\in W^{1,2}(\mathbb{R}^N)
\)
such that
\begin{equation}\label{Vk:weak:W12}
V_k\rightharpoonup V
\qquad\text{weakly in }W^{1,2}(\mathbb{R}^N).
\end{equation}
Furthermore, by the Rellich--Kondrachov theorem, after passing to
a further subsequence if necessary,
\begin{equation}\label{Vk:local:strong}
V_k\longrightarrow V
\qquad\text{strongly in }L^2_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}^N)
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{Vk:ae}
V_k(x)\longrightarrow V(x)
\qquad\text{for a.e. }x\in\mathbb{R}^N.
\end{equation}

\medskip
\noindent
\textit{Case 2:
$q\in\left(1+\frac1N,1+\frac2N\right]$.}
Set
\[
p_-=
\max\left\{1,\frac{N(q-1)}{q}\right\},
\qquad
p_+=N(q-1).
\]
Thus
\(
1\leqslant p_-<p_+\leqslant2.
\)
Fix one exponent
\(
p_0\in(p_-,p_+)
\)
and, for each $k$, choose a solution
\(
V_k\in W^{1,p_0}_0(B_k)
\)
of problem \eqref{Vk_equ:correct} provided by Lemma \ref{lemma_2}.

            
                                                
                                                    
                                                            
                                                           
                                                                              
                                                                       
                                                                               
                                                                                
                                           

Since $B_k$ is bounded, standard elliptic bootstrap applied to equation
\eqref{Vk_equ:correct} shows that each such $V_k$ belongs, in
particular, to
\(
W^{1,p}_0(B_k)
\)
for every finite $p>1$. Thus Lemma \ref{C_psi_1} can be applied
to the same solution $V_k$ for every
\(
p\in(p_-,p_+).
\)
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      
Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{Vk:all:p:bound}
\|V_k\|_{W^{1,p}(\mathbb{R}^N)}
\leqslant C_p
\qquad
\text{for every }p\in(p_-,p_+),
\end{equation}
where $C_p$ is independent of $k$.

Let $\{p_j\}_{j=1}^\infty$ be a countable dense subset of
$(p_-,p_+)$. By reflexivity and a diagonal argument, there exist
a subsequence, still denoted by $\{V_k\}$, and functions
$V^{(j)}\in W^{1,p_j}(\mathbb{R}^N)$ such that
\[
V_k\rightharpoonup V^{(j)}
\qquad\text{weakly in }W^{1,p_j}(\mathbb{R}^N)
\]
for every $j$.
The
Rellich--Kondrachov theorem yields, after another diagonal
extraction,
\[
V_k\longrightarrow V
\qquad\text{strongly in }L^1_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}^N)
\]
and
\[
V_k(x)\longrightarrow V(x)
\qquad\text{for a.e. }x\in\mathbb{R}^N.
\]
Hence all the weak limits $V^{(j)}$ coincide with the same
function $V$. Therefore
\[
V\in W^{1,p_j}(\mathbb{R}^N)
\qquad\text{for every }j.
\]

We claim that, in fact,
\begin{equation}\label{V:all:p}
V\in W^{1,p}(\mathbb{R}^N)
\qquad\text{for every }p\in(p_-,p_+).
\end{equation}
Indeed, fix such a $p$. Choose $p_i,p_j$ from the dense sequence
so that
\(
p_i<p<p_j.
\)
Since
\(
V\in W^{1,p_i}(\mathbb{R}^N)\cap W^{1,p_j}(\mathbb{R}^N),
\)
the interpolation inequality applied both to $V$ and to
$\nabla V$ gives
\(
V\in W^{1,p}(\mathbb{R}^N).
\)


It remains to show that the limit $V$ is a weak solution of
\eqref{ell_V:gen}. The argument is the same in both cases.

Fix
\(
\varphi\in C^\infty_c(\mathbb{R}^N).
\)
For all sufficiently large $k$,
\(
\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subset B_k.
\)
The weak formulation of problem \eqref{Vk_equ:correct} therefore gives
\begin{equation}\label{Vk:weak:form}
\begin{split}
&
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\nabla V_k\cdot\nabla\varphi\,\mathrm d x
-
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}
\frac{x}{2}\cdot\nabla V_k\,\varphi\,\mathrm d x
-
\frac{1}{2(q-1)}
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}V_k\varphi\,\mathrm d x
\\
&\qquad
=
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}
\psi(V_k+U_0)\partial_{x_1}\varphi\,\mathrm d x.
\end{split}
\end{equation}

Choose an exponent $p>1$ for which the sequence $\{V_k\}$ is
bounded in $W^{1,p}(\mathbb{R}^N)$; in Case 1 we take $p=2$, while in
Case 2 we may take any $p\in(p_-,p_+)$. The weak convergence in
$W^{1,p}(\mathbb{R}^N)$ implies
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\nabla V_k\cdot\nabla\varphi\,\mathrm d x
\longrightarrow
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\nabla V\cdot\nabla\varphi\,\mathrm d x,
\]
and, since $x\varphi$ has compact support,
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}
\frac{x}{2}\cdot\nabla V_k\,\varphi\,\mathrm d x
\longrightarrow
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}
\frac{x}{2}\cdot\nabla V\,\varphi\,\mathrm d x.
\]
Similarly,
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}V_k\varphi\,\mathrm d x
\longrightarrow
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}V\varphi\,\mathrm d x.
\]

On the other hand, by the almost everywhere convergence
\eqref{Vk:ae}, or its counterpart in Case 2, and the continuity of
$\psi$,
\[
\psi(V_k+U_0)
\longrightarrow
\psi(V+U_0)
\qquad\text{a.e. in }\mathbb{R}^N.
\]
Moreover,
\[
|\psi(V_k+U_0)\partial_{x_1}\varphi|
\leqslant
\|\psi\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R})}
|\partial_{x_1}\varphi|,
\]
and the right-hand side is integrable because $\varphi$ has compact
support. Hence, by the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem,
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}
\psi(V_k+U_0)\partial_{x_1}\varphi\,\mathrm d x
\longrightarrow
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}
\psi(V+U_0)\partial_{x_1}\varphi\,\mathrm d x.
\]

Passing to the limit in \eqref{Vk:weak:form}, we conclude that
$V$ is a weak solution of equation \eqref{ell_V:gen}, namely, it satisfies relation
\eqref{vf_V:gen}.

label: thm:uniform:estimates
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:uniform:estimates}
Assume that $N\geqslant1$ and
\[
1+\frac1N<q
\quad\text{if }N\in\{1,2\},
\qquad
1+\frac1N<q<\frac{N}{N-2}
\quad\text{if }N\geqslant3.
\]
Let $\psi=\psi_A$ be the truncated nonlinearity defined by
\eqref{psi1}, with an arbitrary truncation level $A>0$. Let
\(
U_0=e^\Delta u_0,
\)
where the homogeneous function $u_0$ is given by \eqref{u0}. Let
$V$ be the whole-space weak solution of \eqref{ell_V:gen}
constructed in Theorem \ref{existence_I}. Then
\(
V\in L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^N)
\)
and
\begin{equation}\label{V:Linfty}
\|V\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^N)}
\leqslant C(N,q,U_0),
\end{equation}
where the constant is independent of the truncation level $A$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $B_k$ be the approximating balls and let $V_k$ be the
corresponding solutions of the bounded-domain problems 
\eqref{Vk_equ}
used in
the proof of Theorem \ref{existence_I}. 
       
                                            
                 
                                        
                      
                                   
                    
        
                           
               
                
After passing to a subsequence, these approximations converge
locally to the whole-space solution $V$ constructed in Theorem
\ref{existence_I}. 
We now prove estimates for $V_k$ that are independent
of both $k$ and the truncation level $A>0$.
In the following, for each $k$, we use the function 
\(
U_k=V_k+U_0.
\)
Since $U_0$ satisfies the linear elliptic equation \eqref{eq:U0:A} below,
    
                                        
                        
                          
    
the function $U_k$ solves
\begin{equation}\label{Uk:bounded:theorem}
\begin{aligned}
-\Delta U_k-\frac{x}{2}\cdot\nabla U_k
-\frac{1}{2(q-1)}U_k
+\partial_{x_1}\psi_A(U_k)&=0
&&\text{in }B_k,\\
U_k&=U_0
&&\text{on }\partial B_k.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

We distinguish four cases.

\medskip
\noindent
\textit{Case 1: $N=1$.}
The condition on $q$ becomes $q>2$. Applying
Lemma \ref{lem:uniform-Linfty-N1} (see below) to $V_k$, we obtain
\[
\|V_k\|_{L^\infty(B_k)}
\leqslant C(q,U_0),
\]
where the constant is independent of $k$ and $A$. Passing to the
whole-space limit gives inequality \eqref{V:Linfty}.
    
                         
                     
    

\medskip
\noindent
\textit{Case 2: $N\geqslant2$ and
$q>1+\frac{1}{N-1}$.}
                                                                        
                                                                        
                                                                               
                                            
The bounded-domain solutions have the regularity required in
Lemma \ref{lem:Linfty}. Applying that lemma to $U_k$, which solves
\eqref{Uk:bounded:theorem}, gives
\[
\|U_k\|_{L^\infty(B_k)}
\leqslant C(N,q,U_0),
\]
where the constant is independent of $k$ and of the nonlinearity
$\psi_A$, and hence independent of $A$.
The heat-profile estimate in Lemma \ref{heat_L} gives
\(
\|U_0\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^N)}
\leqslant C(N,q,U_0).
\)
Therefore,
\[
\|V_k\|_{L^\infty(B_k)}
\leqslant
\|U_k\|_{L^\infty(B_k)}
+\|U_0\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^N)}
\leqslant C(N,q,U_0).
\]
Passing to the limit yields
\[
\|V\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^N)}
\leqslant C(N,q,U_0).
\]


\medskip
\noindent
\textit{Case 3: $N\geqslant2$, $q<2$, and
$q\leqslant1+\frac{1}{N-1}$.}
Under the assumptions of the theorem, this remaining range
satisfies
\[
1+\frac1N<q\leqslant1+\frac2N,
\qquad q<2.
\]
Indeed, if $N\geqslant3$, then
\[
1+\frac{1}{N-1}<1+\frac2N<2,
\]
whereas for $N=2$ the inequality $q<2$ is part of the present case.

Choose, once and for all,
\begin{equation}\label{p:choice:uniform:theorem}
\max\left\{
1,\frac{N(q-1)}q
\right\}
<p<N(q-1).
\end{equation}
Such a choice is possible because $q>1+1/N$. By the
truncation-independent part of Lemma \ref{C_psi_1},
\begin{equation}\label{Vk:uniform:W1p:theorem}
\|V_k\|_{W^{1,p}(B_k)}
\leqslant C(N,q,p,U_0),
\end{equation}
where the constant is independent of $k$ and $A$.

Extend $V_k$ by zero outside $B_k$. Since
$V_k\in W^{1,p}_0(B_k)$, its zero extension belongs to
$W^{1,p}(\mathbb{R}^N)$, and \eqref{Vk:uniform:W1p:theorem} remains
valid on $\mathbb{R}^N$. By weak compactness and the convergence used
in Theorem \ref{existence_I}, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{V:uniform:W1p:theorem}
\|V\|_{W^{1,p}(\mathbb{R}^N)}
\leqslant C(N,q,p,U_0).
\end{equation}

Because
\(
p<N(q-1)\leqslant2\leqslant N,
\)
we have $p<N$. The Sobolev inequality therefore gives
\begin{equation}\label{V:pstar:theorem}
\|V\|_{L^{p^*}(\mathbb{R}^N)}
\leqslant
C(N,p)\|V\|_{W^{1,p}(\mathbb{R}^N)}
\leqslant C(N,q,p,U_0),
\end{equation}
where
\(
p^*=\frac{Np}{N-p}.
\)
Moreover,
\(p^*>N(q-1).
\)
Indeed, by a direct calculation
\begin{align*}
p^*>N(q-1) \quad \text{is equivalent to} \quad
p>\frac{N(q-1)}q,
\end{align*}
which follows from \eqref{p:choice:uniform:theorem}.

By Lemma \ref{heat_L},
\(
U_0\in L^{p^*}(\mathbb{R}^N)
\)
because $p^*>N(q-1)$. Consequently, for
\(
U=V+U_0,
\)
we have
\begin{equation}\label{U:pstar:theorem}
\|U\|_{L^{p^*}(\mathbb{R}^N)}
\leqslant
\|V\|_{L^{p^*}(\mathbb{R}^N)}
+\|U_0\|_{L^{p^*}(\mathbb{R}^N)}
\leqslant C(N,q,p,U_0),
\end{equation}
uniformly with respect to $A$.
Now, 
Lemma \ref{lem:large:p:U}, applied with $p_0=p^*$, yields
\[
\|U\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^N)}
\leqslant
C(N,q,p^*)\|U\|_{L^{p^*}(\mathbb{R}^N)}
\leqslant C(N,q,U_0).
\]
The constant in Lemma \ref{lem:large:p:U} is independent of the
nonlinearity and therefore independent of $A$. Finally,
\[
\|V\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^N)}
\leqslant
\|U\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^N)}
+\|U_0\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^N)}
\leqslant C(N,q,U_0).
\]


\medskip
\noindent
\textit{Case 4: $N=2$ and $q=2$.} Use
Lemma~\ref{lem:uniform:Linfty:N2:q2}, below.
head: environment

label: lem:uniform-Linfty-N1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:uniform-Linfty-N1}
Let \(q>2\) and let \(\Omega=(a,b)\subset\mathbb R\). Suppose that
\(u_0:\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\to\mathbb R\) is homogeneous of
degree \(-1/(q-1)\)
          
    
                
   
                                
        
                                                      
    
and set $U_0=e^\Delta u_0$.
Let $\psi$ be the truncated nonlinearity 
\eqref{psi1} with an arbitrary truncation level $A>0$.
Suppose that \(V\in W^{1,2}_0(a,b)\) is a weak solution of the ordinary differential equation
\begin{equation}
\label{ell:bounded:N1}
-V''-\frac{x}{2}V'
-\frac{1}{2(q-1)}V
+\frac{d}{dx}\psi_A(V+U_0)=0
\qquad\text{in }(a,b).
\end{equation}
Then
\[
\|V\|_{L^\infty(a,b)}
\leqslant C(q,u_0),
\]
where the constant is independent of \(A\) and of the interval
\((a,b)\).
head: environment
name: Uniform one-dimensional \(L^\infty\) estimate

title: Proof
body_md:
Set
\[
c=\frac{1}{2(q-1)},
\qquad
\beta=\frac12-c>0,
\qquad
B=\|U_0\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb R)},
\]
and define
\[
K=\frac{q}{\beta}
\int_{\mathbb R}|U_0|^{q-1}|U_0'|\,dx.
\]
The heat-profile estimates imply that $B,K<\infty$.
Indeed,
\[
|U_0(x)|^{q-1}|U_0'(x)|
\leqslant
C(q,u_0)(1+|x|)^{-q/(q-1)},
\]
and $q/(q-1)>1$.

Since $\psi_A$ is globally Lipschitz, the equation gives
$V\in W^{2,2}(a,b)\subset C^1([a,b])$.
We first prove that
\begin{equation}
\label{N1:uniform:L1}
\|V\|_{L^1(a,b)}\leqslant K.
\end{equation}
Let $I=(\ell,r)$ be a connected component of $\{V\neq0\}$,
and let $\sigma\in\{-1,1\}$ be the sign of $V$ on $I$.
Integrating \eqref{ell:bounded:N1} over $I$ and multiplying
by $\sigma$, we obtain
\[
-\sigma[V']_\ell^r
+\beta\int_I|V|\,dx
=
-\sigma[\psi_A(U_0)]_\ell^r.
\]
Here $V(\ell)=V(r)=0$ and
$-\sigma[V']_\ell^r\geqslant0$. Consequently,
\[
\beta\int_I|V|\,dx
\leqslant
\int_I|(\psi_A(U_0))'|\,dx.
\]
Summing over the components and using
$|\psi_A'(s)|\leqslant q|s|^{q-1}$ proves
\eqref{N1:uniform:L1}.

Now set $U=V+U_0$. Since
\[
-U_0''-\frac{x}{2}U_0'-cU_0=0,
\]
we have
\[
-U''-\frac{x}{2}U'-cU+(\psi_A(U))'=0
\qquad\text{in }(a,b),
\]
with $U=U_0$ at the endpoints.
Define
\[
w=(|U|-B)_+.
\]
Then $w\in W^{1,2}_0(a,b)$ and $0\leqslant w\leqslant|V|$,
so \eqref{N1:uniform:L1} gives
\[
\|w\|_{L^1(a,b)}\leqslant K.
\]

Test the equation for $U$ with $\operatorname{sgn}(U)w$.
The convection term vanishes: its integrand is the derivative
of $P_A(U)$, where
\[
P_A(s)=
\int_0^s
\psi_A'(t)\operatorname{sgn}(t)(|t|-B)_+\,dt,
\]
and $P_A(U(a))=P_A(U(b))=0$.
Integration by parts therefore yields
\[
\|w'\|_2^2+
\left(\frac14-c\right)\|w\|_2^2
=
cB\|w\|_1,
\]
where all norms are taken over $(a,b)$.
Writing 
$$M=\|w\|_\infty,$$ we deduce that
\begin{equation}
\label{N1:excess:energy}
\|w'\|_2^2
\leqslant c\|w\|_2^2+cB\|w\|_1
\leqslant cK(M+B).
\end{equation}

Finally, since $w(a)=0$, the fundamental theorem of calculus
and the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality give
\[
w(x)^{3/2}
=
\frac32\int_a^x w^{1/2}w'\,dy
\leqslant
\frac32\|w\|_1^{1/2}\|w'\|_2.
\]
Taking the supremum and using \eqref{N1:excess:energy},
we obtain
\[
M^3
\leqslant
\frac94K\|w'\|_2^2
\leqslant
\frac{9c}{4}K^2(M+B).
\]
Thus either $M\leqslant B$, or
$M\leqslant3\sqrt{c/2}\,K$.
Since $|V|\leqslant|U|+B\leqslant w+2B$, it follows that
\[
\|V\|_{L^\infty(a,b)}
\leqslant
3B+3\sqrt{\frac c2}\,K
=
C(q,u_0).
\]
The right-hand side is independent of $A$ and $(a,b)$.

head: environment

label: U:linearized
title: Proof
body_md:
Set
\[
a=\frac{1}{q-1},
\qquad
c=\frac{a}{2}=\frac{1}{2(q-1)}.
\]
By the Sobolev chain rule,
\(
\partial_{x_1}\psi(U)
=
\psi'(U)\partial_{x_1}U
\)
a.e.~in $\Omega$.
Consequently, equation \eqref{U:bounded} can be written as
\begin{equation}
\label{U:linearized}
-\Delta U+
\left(
\psi'(U)e_1-\frac{x}{2}
\right)\cdot\nabla U
-cU=0
\qquad\text{in }\Omega.
\end{equation}

Write
\(
x=(x_1,x'),
\)
where
\(
x'\in\mathbb{R}^{N-1},
\)
and define
\begin{equation}
\label{Phi:definition}
\Phi(x')
=
e^{\Delta_{\mathbb{R}^{N-1}}}|x'|^{-a}
=
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{N-1}}
G_{N-1}(x'-y,1)|y|^{-a}\,\,\mathrm d y,
\end{equation}
where $G_{N-1}$ denotes the heat kernel for the heat equation on $\mathbb{R}^{N-1}.$
Condition \eqref{q:maximum} gives
\[
0<a<N-1.
\]
Thus, $|x'|^{-a}$ is locally integrable in
$\mathbb{R}^{N-1}$, and, by Lemma \ref{heat_L}, the function $\Phi$ is smooth, strictly positive, and
bounded. Moreover, by Lemma~\ref{heat_L}, it satisfies the linear equation
\begin{equation}
\label{Phi:reduced-equation}
-\Delta_{x'}\Phi
-\frac{x'}{2}\cdot\nabla_{x'}\Phi
-\frac{a}{2}\Phi=0
\qquad\text{in }\mathbb{R}^{N-1}.
\end{equation}
We extend $\Phi$ to $\mathbb{R}^N$ by setting
\(
\Phi(x)=\Phi(x').
\)
Since
\(
\partial_{x_1}\Phi=0
\)
and
\(
c=\frac a2,
\)
equation \eqref{Phi:reduced-equation} implies
\begin{equation}
\label{Phi:equation}
-\Delta\Phi+
\left(
\psi'(U)e_1-\frac{x}{2}
\right)\cdot\nabla\Phi
-c\Phi=0
\qquad\text{in }\Omega.
\end{equation}
The term containing $\psi'(U)$ vanishes because $\Phi$ is
independent of $x_1$.

We next recall the two-sided estimate
\begin{equation}
\label{Phi:two-sided}
\frac{c_0}{1+|x'|^a}
\leqslant
\Phi(x')
\leqslant
\frac{C_0}{1+|x'|^a},
\qquad x'\in\mathbb{R}^{N-1},
\end{equation}
where $c_0,C_0>0$ depend only on $N$ and $q$. 
These estimates follow from the heat-profile asymptotics recalled in
Lemma~\ref{L:A3} below.
The heat-profile estimate recalled in Lemma \ref{heat_L} and applied to $U_0=e^\Delta u_0$ gives 
\[
|U_0(x)|
\leqslant
\frac{C(U_0)}{1+|x|^a}
\leqslant
\frac{C(U_0)}{1+|x'|^a}.
\]
Combining this estimate with the lower bound in
\eqref{Phi:two-sided}, we obtain
\begin{equation}
\label{U0:Phi}
|U_0(x)|
\leqslant
M_0\Phi(x')
\qquad\text{for all }x\in\mathbb{R}^N,
\end{equation}
where $M_0=M_0(N,q,U_0)>0$. In particular, $M_0$ is independent
of $\Omega$ and $\psi$.

Now we define
\[
Z=\frac{U}{\Phi}.
\]
Since $\Omega$ is bounded and $\Phi$ is smooth and strictly
positive on $\overline\Omega$, the function $1/\Phi$ is bounded on
$\Omega$,
    
                               
    
and hence $Z\in W^{1,2}(\Omega)$. Substituting $U=\Phi Z$ into
\eqref{U:linearized} and using \eqref{Phi:equation}, we obtain
\begin{equation}
\label{Z:equation}
-\Delta Z+b(x)\cdot\nabla Z=0
\qquad\text{in }\Omega,
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}\label{b:in:Z:equation}
b(x)
=
\psi'(U)e_1-\frac{x}{2}
-2\frac{\nabla\Phi}{\Phi}.
\end{equation}
This is a standard technique commonly used when applying the maximum principle to elliptic equations with a zero-order term (see, e.g., \cite[Chap.~2, Sec.~5]{PW84}); we therefore omit the calculations leading to equation \eqref{Z:equation}.
             
    
                               
    
                   
    
                                    
        
                                                             
    
                                                                     
                           
    
                        
                                                              
    
                                                       
Note that, for each fixed $\Omega$ and $\psi$, we have
\(
b\in L^\infty(\Omega),
\)
because $\psi'\in L^\infty(\mathbb{R})$, $\Omega$ is bounded, and
$\nabla\Phi/\Phi$ is bounded on $\overline\Omega$.

Both \(Z\) and \(-Z\) are sufficiently regular solutions of the linear elliptic equation \eqref{Z:equation}. Therefore, the weak maximum principle can be applied to obtain
\begin{equation}
\label{Z:maximum}
\|Z\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}
\leqslant
\|Z\|_{L^\infty(\partial\Omega)}.
\end{equation}
By the boundary condition \eqref{U:boundary},
\[
Z=\frac{U_0}{\Phi}
\qquad\text{on }\partial\Omega.
\]
Therefore, estimate \eqref{U0:Phi} gives
\(
|Z|\leqslant M_0
\)
on $\partial\Omega$.
It follows from \eqref{Z:maximum} that
\[
|Z(x)|\leqslant M_0
\qquad\text{for a.e. }x\in\Omega.
\]
Consequently,
\[
|U(x)|
\leqslant
M_0\Phi(x')
\qquad\text{for a.e. }x\in\Omega.
\]
Using the upper bound in \eqref{Phi:two-sided}, we conclude that
    
        
           
                         
                   
    
       
\[
\|U\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}
\leqslant
M_0C_0
=
C(N,q,U_0).
\]
This estimate is independent of the domain $\Omega$ and of the nonlinearity $\psi$.
head: environment

label: lem:large:p:U
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:large:p:U}
Let $N\geqslant1$, $q>1$, and let
$\psi\in W^{1,\infty}(\mathbb{R})$ be arbitrary. Suppose that $U$ is
a sufficiently regular solution of
\begin{equation}\label{ell_U:large:p}
-\Delta U
-\frac12 x\cdot\nabla U
-\frac{1}{2(q-1)}U
+\partial_{x_1}\psi(U)=0
\qquad\text{in }\mathbb{R}^N,
\end{equation}
such that the integrations by parts below are justified. Assume
that
\[
U\in L^{p_0}(\mathbb{R}^N)
\qquad\text{for some}\qquad
p_0>\max\{1,N(q-1)\}.
\]
Then
    
                   
                                          
    
      
there exists a constant $C=C(N,q,p_0)>0$, independent of
$\psi$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{U:Linfty:large:p}
\|U\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^N)}
\leqslant
C(N,q,p_0)\|U\|_{L^{p_0}(\mathbb{R}^N)}.
\end{equation}
head: environment

label: large:p:energy
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $p>1$ and assume initially that
$U\in L^p(\mathbb{R}^N)$. Testing equation \eqref{ell_U:large:p} with
$|U|^{p-2}U$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{large:p:energy}
\frac{4(p-1)}{p^2}
\left\|\nabla |U|^{p/2}\right\|_2^2
+
\left(
\frac{N}{2p}-\frac{1}{2(q-1)}
\right)\|U\|_p^p
=0.
\end{equation}
In this calculation, we use the following two identities obtained by
integration by parts:
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}
 \partial_{x_1}\psi(U)|U|^{p-2}U\,\,\mathrm d x
=0
\]
and
\[
-\frac12
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}
x\cdot\nabla U\,|U|^{p-2}U\,\,\mathrm d x
=
-\frac{1}{2p}
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}x\cdot\nabla(|U|^p)\,\,\mathrm d x
=
\frac{N}{2p}\|U\|_p^p.
\]
This calculation may be justified by first using regularized
powers and compactly supported cutoff functions and then passing
to the limit. Notice that
no estimate involving $\psi$ remains in the energy
identity \eqref{large:p:energy}.

                                   
                                                     
    
        
   
          
                                       
    
                                   
                                  
          
           
                                  
                
                                                           
                     
    
                      
   
                                     
   
                                 
    
                    

                                             
    
                                   
                                
                                  
        
                                     
    
      
                
                
                                              
    
                
                                     
    
                 
                                    
              
                      
    
        
                
                                   
         
           
                              
                                        
                   
    
                                                      






                          

                                


    
          
                
                                   
   
               
                                          
   
                        
    
            
                                        
                    
                                     
   
        
                               
                  
     
                

If $p>N(q-1)$, set
\[
\beta_p
=
\frac{1}{2(q-1)}-\frac{N}{2p}>0.
\]
Then equation \eqref{large:p:energy} becomes
\begin{equation}\label{large:p:gradient:exact}
\left\|\nabla |U|^{p/2}\right\|_2^2
=
D_p\|U\|_p^p,
\qquad
D_p
=
\frac{p^2}{4(p-1)}\beta_p.
\end{equation}
                                       
Moreover, for $p\geqslant2$,
\[
D_p
\leqslant
\frac{p^2}{8(q-1)(p-1)}
\leqslant
\frac{p}{4(q-1)},
\]
which proves                       
\begin{equation}\label{large:p:grad}
\left\|\nabla |U|^{p/2}\right\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)}^2
\leqslant
C(q)p\|U\|_{L^p(\mathbb{R}^N)}^p.
\end{equation}

We now bootstrap the integrability of $U$.

\medskip
\noindent
\textit{Case 1: $N\geqslant3$.}
Set
\[
\kappa=\frac{N}{N-2}.
\]
Applying the Sobolev inequality to
$w=|U|^{p/2}$ and using
\eqref{large:p:gradient:exact}, we obtain
\[
\|U\|_{\kappa p}^p
=
\left\||U|^{p/2}\right\|_{\frac{2N}{N-2}}^2
\leqslant
C(N)\left\|\nabla |U|^{p/2}\right\|_2^2
=
C(N)D_p\|U\|_p^p.
\]
Hence
\begin{equation}\label{large:p:iteration:step}
\|U\|_{\kappa p}
\leqslant
\bigl(C(N)D_p\bigr)^{1/p}\|U\|_p.
\end{equation}

Let
\(
p_j=\kappa^jp_0.
\)
Since $p_j\geqslant p_0>1$,
\[
D_{p_j}\leqslant C(q,p_0)p_j.
\]
Iterating \eqref{large:p:iteration:step} yields
\[
\|U\|_{p_m}
\leqslant
\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}
\bigl(C(N)D_{p_j}\bigr)^{1/p_j}
\|U\|_{p_0}.
\]
The product is bounded uniformly in $m$ because
\[
\sum_{j=0}^\infty
\frac{\log\bigl(\max\{1,C(N)D_{p_j}\}\bigr)}{p_j}
\leqslant
C\sum_{j=0}^\infty
\frac{1+\log p_j}{p_j}
<\infty.
\]
Since $p_m\to\infty$, it follows that
\(
\|U\|_\infty
\leqslant
C(N,q,p_0)\|U\|_{p_0}.
\)

\medskip
\noindent
\textit{Case 2: $N=2$.}
The Gagliardo--Nirenberg inequality gives
\[
\|w\|_4^2
\leqslant
C\|w\|_2\|\nabla w\|_2.
\]
Taking $w=|U|^{p/2}$ and using
\eqref{large:p:gradient:exact}, we obtain
\[
\|U\|_{2p}^p
\leqslant
C\|U\|_p^{p/2}
\left\|\nabla |U|^{p/2}\right\|_2
=
CD_p^{1/2}\|U\|_p^p.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\|U\|_{2p}
\leqslant
\bigl(CD_p^{1/2}\bigr)^{1/p}\|U\|_p.
\]
Taking $p_j=2^jp_0$ and iterating as above gives
\[
\|U\|_\infty
\leqslant
C(q,p_0)\|U\|_{p_0}.
\]

\medskip
\noindent
\textit{Case 3: $N=1$.}
Using the inequality
\(
\|w\|_\infty^2
\leqslant
C\|w\|_2\|w'\|_2
\)
with $w=|U|^{p_0/2}$, we obtain
\begin{align*}
\|U\|_\infty^{p_0}
\leqslant
C\|U\|_{p_0}^{p_0/2}
\left\|\partial_x|U|^{p_0/2}\right\|_2
=
CD_{p_0}^{1/2}\|U\|_{p_0}^{p_0}.
\end{align*}
Consequently,
\[
\|U\|_\infty
\leqslant
\bigl(CD_{p_0}^{1/2}\bigr)^{1/p_0}
\|U\|_{p_0}
\leqslant
C(q,p_0)\|U\|_{p_0}.
\]

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $V=V_k$ and set
\[
D=\|\partial_{x_1}U_0\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^2)},
\qquad
F=|U_0\partial_{x_1}U_0|.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{heat_L},
\[
|U_0(x)|+|\nabla U_0(x)|
\leqslant \frac{C(U_0)}{1+|x|}.
\]
Hence $D<\infty$ and
\[
F(x)\leqslant \frac{C(U_0)}{(1+|x|)^2},
\qquad
F\in L^s(\mathbb{R}^2)
\quad\text{for every }s>1.
\]

For each fixed $A$ and $k$, the boundedness of $\psi_A'$
and elliptic bootstrap give
$V\in W^{2,t}(B_k)$ for every finite $t>1$.
Thus the regularized power tests below are admissible.
The constants in this preliminary regularity argument
need not be uniform in $A$ or $k$.

For $1<s<2$, set
\[
w_s=|V|^{s/2-1}V,
\qquad
\alpha_s=\frac{4(s-1)}{s^2},
\qquad
\beta_s=\frac1s-\frac12.
\]
Unless otherwise indicated, norms of $V$ and $w_s$ are
taken over $B_k$.

Testing \eqref{endpoint:N2:q2:bounded} with
\[
\Phi_{s,\delta}(V)
=
V(V^2+\delta)^{(s-2)/2},
\]
integrating the convection term by parts, and letting
$\delta\downarrow0$, we obtain
\begin{align}
\alpha_s\|\nabla w_s\|_2^2
+\beta_s\|V\|_s^s
&\leqslant
\int_{B_k}|\partial_{x_1}U_0|
\left|
(s-1)\int_0^V
\psi_A'(z+U_0)|z|^{s-2}\,\,\mathrm d z
\right|\,\mathrm d x.
\label{endpoint:power:energy}
\end{align}
To justify the nonlinear integration by parts, use the
primitive
\[
P_{s,\delta}(v,u)
=
\int_0^v
\psi_A(z+u)\Phi_{s,\delta}'(z)\,\,\mathrm d z.
\]
Since $P_{s,\delta}(0,u)=0$ and $V=0$ on $\partial B_k$,
\[
\int_{B_k}
\psi_A(V+U_0)\Phi_{s,\delta}'(V)
\partial_{x_1}V\,\,\mathrm d x
=
-\int_{B_k}
\partial_uP_{s,\delta}(V,U_0)
\partial_{x_1}U_0\,\,\mathrm d x.
\]
Dominated convergence applies to the latter integral,
while Fatou's lemma gives the diffusion term in
\eqref{endpoint:power:energy}.

The bound $|\psi_A'(z)|\leqslant 2|z|$ gives
\begin{align*}
\left|
(s-1)\int_0^v
\psi_A'(z+u)|z|^{s-2}\,\,\mathrm d z
\right|
&\leqslant
2(s-1)\int_0^{|v|}
(z+|u|)z^{s-2}\,\,\mathrm d z\\
&=
\frac{2(s-1)}s|v|^s
+2|u||v|^{s-1}.
\end{align*}
Consequently, by H\"older's inequality,
\begin{equation}
\label{endpoint:basic:estimate}
\alpha_s\|\nabla w_s\|_2^2
+\beta_s\|V\|_s^s
\leqslant
\frac{2(s-1)}s D\|V\|_s^s
+
2\|F\|_{L^s(\mathbb{R}^2)}\|V\|_s^{s-1}.
\end{equation}
The factor $s-1$ in the first term on the right-hand side
allows us to absorb this term by choosing $s$ close to $1$.

Choose an auxiliary exponent
\[
1<r<
\min\left\{
p,\,
1+\frac{1}{1+4D}
\right\}.
\]
Then
\[
\gamma_r
:=
\beta_r-\frac{2(r-1)}rD
=
\frac{2-r-4D(r-1)}{2r}
>0.
\]
Applying \eqref{endpoint:basic:estimate} with $s=r$
and using Young's inequality, we obtain
\begin{align*}
\alpha_r\|\nabla w_r\|_2^2
+\gamma_r\|V\|_r^r
&\leqslant
2\|F\|_{L^r(\mathbb{R}^2)}\|V\|_r^{r-1}\\
&\leqslant
\frac{\gamma_r}{2}\|V\|_r^r+C(p,U_0).
\end{align*}
Therefore,
\[
\|\nabla w_r\|_2^2+\|V\|_r^r
\leqslant C(p,U_0).
\]
Lemma~\ref{lemma_1} now yields
\begin{equation}
\label{endpoint:auxiliary:W1r}
\|V\|_{W^{1,r}(B_k)}
\leqslant C(p,U_0),
\end{equation}
uniformly in $A$ and $k$.

Extend $V$ by zero outside $B_k$.
Since $V\in W^{1,r}_0(B_k)$, the Sobolev inequality
on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and \eqref{endpoint:auxiliary:W1r} imply
\[
\|V\|_{L^{r^*}(\mathbb{R}^2)}
\leqslant C(p,U_0),
\qquad
r^*=\frac{2r}{2-r}>2.
\]
Because $r<p<2<r^*$, interpolation gives
\begin{equation}
\label{endpoint:uniform:Lp}
\|V\|_{L^p(B_k)}
\leqslant C(p,U_0).
\end{equation}

Returning to \eqref{endpoint:basic:estimate} with $s=p$
and using \eqref{endpoint:uniform:Lp}, we obtain
\[
\|\nabla w_p\|_2^2
\leqslant C(p,U_0).
\]
A second application of Lemma~\ref{lemma_1} gives
\[
\|V\|_{W^{1,p}(B_k)}^p
\leqslant
C(p)\left(
\|\nabla w_p\|_2^2+\|V\|_p^p
\right)
\leqslant C(p,U_0),
\]
which proves \eqref{endpoint:N2:q2:W1p}.

Finally, apply the estimate with $p=3/2$.
After extending $V_k$ by zero and passing to the
whole-space limit, weak lower semicontinuity gives
\[
\|V\|_{W^{1,3/2}(\mathbb{R}^2)}
\leqslant C(U_0).
\]
The Sobolev embedding
$W^{1,3/2}(\mathbb{R}^2)\hookrightarrow L^6(\mathbb{R}^2)$
therefore yields
\[
\|V\|_{L^6(\mathbb{R}^2)}
\leqslant C(U_0).
\]
Since $U_0\in L^6(\mathbb{R}^2)\cap L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^2)$,
the whole-space profile $U=V+U_0$ satisfies
\[
\|U\|_{L^6(\mathbb{R}^2)}
\leqslant C(U_0).
\]
Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:large:p:U} to $U$ with $p_0=6$,
we obtain
\[
\|U\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^2)}
\leqslant
C\|U\|_{L^6(\mathbb{R}^2)}
\leqslant C(U_0),
\]
where the constant is independent of $\psi_A$ and hence
of $A$. Thus
\[
\|V\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^2)}
\leqslant
\|U\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^2)}
+\|U_0\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^2)}
\leqslant C(U_0).
\]
